The ‘t' is often silent in English when it comes in the middle of words, and sometimes at the end.
When you pronounce these words, you soften the sound or leave it out altogether.
Pronounce these words that soften the ‘t' sound.
Pronounce these words that leave out the ‘t' sound.
I hate being jostled in the crowd, listening to everyone talking about the next best thing.
As I hasten along, looking for my favorite kitchen store, I am reminded of Christmas.
When a word that ends with a consonant plus t is linked to a word that begins with a consonant, you often drop the final t at the end of the first word.
When you delete or drop the final t, the consonant sound before the t links smoothly into the next word.
You must be starving = You mus_be starving

When have follows must, have is reduced to _uv or _a.
The ‘t' sound joins the reduced have.
must have = mus_tuv or mus_ta

images.text: “Why is the mall so crowded today?” I ask myself. I look at my watch and wonder, “Why so early, too?” Oh no! Today must be the day the latest gadgets are being released at the computer store. I must have forgotten to mark it on my calendar!

I hate being jostled in the crowd, listening to everyone talking about the next best thing. As I hasten through them, looking for my favorite kitchen store, I am reminded of Christmas shopping crowds. I must find a way through the seething mass of laptop, notebook, cellphone, and tablet lovers!
Everyone must be here today! I mustn't panic. I must just hustle along, head down until I catch a glimpse of the gourmet shop I want to visit. Once inside, there are no more crowds to wrestle.
The din softens. I must be the only one here, standing among the glistening pots and pans. I breathe a sigh of relief and turn to take in the sea of modern cooking utensils. This must be heaven!
